explanations.explanation: That's the ask. He says, “…give me understanding to learn Your commandments.” Notice he doesn't ask for a shortcut. He asks for the kind of understanding that lets him learn them. A good student goes straight to the Maker for that.

explanations.answer: Strength to defeat all his enemies
explanations.explanation: I get why this one pulls at you, because enemies do show up later in this psalm. But right here, the psalmist asks for something different. He says, “…give me understanding to learn Your commandments.” Nothing about defeating anybody in this verse, friend.

explanations.answer: Riches to take care of his family
explanations.explanation: Riches and family never come up in this verse. The psalmist is talking to the One whose hands made him, and what he asks for is “…understanding to learn Your commandments.” That's the whole request. I'd say a man who asks for understanding before anything else has his priorities in the right order.
Word is it. He says, “…for I have hoped in Your word.” His hope isn't sitting in a person or a plan. It's sitting in what God has said. That's a sturdy place to put your weight.

No temple in this verse, friend. The psalmist says, “…for I have hoped in Your word.” His hope is in what God has spoken, not in a building. I've seen buildings get worn down, believe me, so the word is the better bet.
Armies would make this a very different psalm. Here the psalmist says, “…for I have hoped in Your word.” There's no soldier in sight. His hope rests on what God has said.

True. He says, “…in faithfulness You have afflicted me.” That's a hard thing to say out loud, and he says it right next to “I know, O LORD, that Your judgments are righteous.” He calls the LORD faithful even in the hard season. I think that took real honesty.

The text says the opposite. The psalmist says, “…in faithfulness You have afflicted me.” So he does say it, and he says it while calling the LORD's judgments righteous. It's a surprising line, and that's exactly why it's worth a second look.

Yes, he says, “May Your compassion come to me, that I may live…” He's asking for compassion so that he may live. I think he knows he needs it. Then he gives his reason in the same verse, which comes up in the next question.

No land in this verse, friend. The psalmist says, “May Your compassion come to me, that I may live…” It's about him living, and he asks for it plainly. Healing a whole land would be a different prayer.
Home never comes up here. He asks, “May Your compassion come to me, that I may live…” That's the whole point of the compassion in this verse: that he may live. The verse says nothing about a trip.
Delight. He says, “…for Your law is my delight.” Some people hear the word law and picture a chore list. For this psalmist it's the thing he enjoys. Now THAT is a different outlook, baker.
I know the word law can sound heavy. But the psalmist says, “…for Your law is my delight.” Delight, not burden. He's smiling about it, friend.
Secret doesn't show up here. The psalmist says, “…for Your law is my delight.” He isn't tucking it away. He's saying out loud that he loves it.

That's his answer to the lie. He says, “I will meditate on Your precepts.” The arrogant are subverting him with a lie, and his move is to think deeply on what God has said. He doesn't spend that verse planning anything against them.

That's what many of us would want to do, I'll admit it. But the psalmist doesn't say he will pay anyone back. He asks that the arrogant be put to shame, and then says, “I will meditate on Your precepts.” He leaves the shaming to God and keeps his own mind on God's word.
No packing of bags in this verse. The psalmist says, “I will meditate on Your precepts.” The lie is aimed at him, and his response is to think on God's word. He doesn't mention leaving anywhere.
It's actually the reverse. The psalmist says, “May those who fear You turn to me, those who know Your testimonies.” Turn TO him, not away. He wants those people close.

False, and you read it right. He says, “May those who fear You turn to me, those who know Your testimonies.” He's asking for those people to come near him, not walk off. After all the liars in this stretch, I think he wants some good company.

explanations.answer: So he won't be put to shame
explanations.explanation: The verse gives the reason itself. He says, “May my heart be blameless in Your statutes, that I may not be put to shame.” The heart comes first, and the shame is what he hopes to avoid. He's asking about the inside, not just the outside.

explanations.answer: So kings will give him honor
explanations.explanation: Kings aren't mentioned anywhere in this verse. The psalmist says, “May my heart be blameless in Your statutes, that I may not be put to shame.” His reason is not being put to shame. Nobody's handing out honors here.

explanations.answer: So he'll grow rich in old age
explanations.explanation: Old age and money never come up. The psalmist says, “May my heart be blameless in Your statutes, that I may not be put to shame.” The verse names one reason, and it's the shame. Anything beyond that, the text doesn't say.

Yes. He asks, “When will You comfort me?” Right before that, he says his eyes are looking for God's promise. It's an honest question, asked straight to the LORD. And being honest like that is something this psalm does over and over.

explanations.answer: Why did You ever make me
explanations.explanation: That's a sad question, but the psalmist doesn't ask it here. He asks, “When will You comfort me?” He's waiting, and what he wants is comfort. Earlier in this psalm he said God's hands made him, so this question wouldn't match.

explanations.answer: Where have You gone to now
explanations.explanation: That's not what he asks. The text says, “When will You comfort me?” He's looking for God's promise, and the question is about comfort and timing. He doesn't say God has gone anywhere.

Close, but it's the other way around. The psalmist says, “Though I am like a wineskin dried up by smoke, I do not forget Your statutes.” He looks worn out, and he still holds on. That little word “Though” is carrying a lot.
False. He says, “Though I am like a wineskin dried up by smoke, I do not forget Your statutes.” He's dried up and still remembering. Feeling worn out didn't wipe God's word from his mind.

explanations.answer: When God will judge his persecutors
explanations.explanation: That's the second question. He asks, “How many days must Your servant wait? When will You execute judgment on my persecutors?” The first is about the waiting, and the second is about his persecutors. He's bringing both to the LORD instead of keeping them inside.

explanations.answer: Why his closest friends have left him
explanations.explanation: Friends leaving isn't mentioned in this verse. After asking how many days he must wait, he asks, “When will You execute judgment on my persecutors?” His question is about his persecutors. The text doesn't give him any friends to lose here.

explanations.answer: Where his family has been taken to
explanations.explanation: His family never appears in this verse. He asks, “How many days must Your servant wait? When will You execute judgment on my persecutors?” The second question is about the persecutors. The text doesn't mention anyone being taken.

explanations.answer: There's no cause for it at all
explanations.explanation: Yes. He says, “I am persecuted without cause—help me!” Without cause means there's no reason for it. And he says it right after calling all of God's commandments faithful. I think that's a heavy thing to carry.

explanations.answer: He broke one of the king's laws
explanations.explanation: The psalmist says nothing like that. He says, “I am persecuted without cause—help me!” Without cause is the opposite of a good reason. A king's law isn't in this verse at all.

explanations.answer: He stole land from his neighbor
explanations.explanation: Land and neighbors never come up here. The psalmist says, “I am persecuted without cause—help me!” He says there's no cause, and the text doesn't give him one. We only know what he says, friend.
True. He says, “They almost wiped me from the earth, but I have not forsaken Your precepts.” They came close, and he still held on. That little word “but” is carrying a lot.
The text says the opposite. The psalmist says, “They almost wiped me from the earth, but I have not forsaken Your precepts.” They almost got him, and he did not forsake them. So the answer is True.
Revive is the first one. He prays, “Revive me according to Your loving devotion…” He's asking for new life, and he's asking according to God's loving devotion. I think that's a good measuring stick.
Obey is the second one. He says, “…that I may obey the testimony of Your mouth.” The reviving has a purpose: obeying what God has said. The prayer goes from new life to following God's word.

Judge shows up in this stretch, but not here. Back in verse 84 he asks when God will execute judgment on his persecutors. In verse 88 the first blank is something he asks for himself: “Revive me according to Your loving devotion…” So this one belongs in a different verse.

Forget is a word the psalmist uses to say what he does NOT do. In verse 83 he says, “I do not forget Your statutes.” Here, in verse 88, he's asking to be revived according to God's loving devotion. So forget doesn't fit either blank.

Silence doesn't appear in this verse. The psalmist asks, “Revive me according to Your loving devotion, that I may obey the testimony of Your mouth.” He wants new life, not a quiet room. So this one is just a cookie that never went in the oven.

explanations.answer: It is everlasting and fixed in the heavens
explanations.explanation: That's the big one. He says, “Your word, O LORD, is everlasting; it is firmly fixed in the heavens.” After all the liars and pits, he looks up at something that doesn't move. God's word stays put when everything else shakes.

explanations.answer: It is hidden and hard for anyone to find
explanations.explanation: The psalmist says the opposite of hidden. He says, “Your word, O LORD, is everlasting; it is firmly fixed in the heavens.” Fixed and everlasting, in plain view of the heavens. Nothing in this verse says it's hard to find.

explanations.answer: It is only for the priests in the temple
explanations.explanation: Priests and temples aren't in this verse. The psalmist says, “Your word, O LORD, is everlasting; it is firmly fixed in the heavens.” He's talking about the word itself and how lasting it is. The verse doesn't say who it's for, so we won't add that.
Almost, but the second half is the problem. The psalmist says, “You established the earth, and it endures.” Endures, not fades. The earth is standing because God established it.
False, and you caught it. The psalmist says, “You established the earth, and it endures.” The first half of the card is true, but the second half isn't. God established it, and it endures.
Servants. He says, “Your ordinances stand to this day, for all things are servants to You.” All things, not just some of them. That's a big sentence, and he says it plainly.

Enemies come up plenty in this psalm, but not in this verse. The psalmist says, “Your ordinances stand to this day, for all things are servants to You.” All things are His servants. That's the opposite of enemies.
Treasures is a nice guess, but it's not the word. The psalmist says, “Your ordinances stand to this day, for all things are servants to You.” Servants is how he describes all things. They serve Him.

explanations.answer: He would have perished in his affliction
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. “If Your law had not been my delight, then I would have perished in my affliction.” He's looking back at the hard stretch and naming what got him through. He doesn't say it lightly, and I think we shouldn't hear it lightly.

explanations.answer: He would have run away from his enemies
explanations.explanation: Running away isn't the word he uses. He says, “If Your law had not been my delight, then I would have perished in my affliction.” Perished is much heavier. The psalmist doesn't say anything about running.

explanations.answer: He would have turned his back on God
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says would have happened. He says, “If Your law had not been my delight, then I would have perished in my affliction.” Elsewhere in this passage he says, “I have not forsaken Your precepts.” (Psalm 119:87). What he says he'd lose here is his life.
True. He says, “I will never forget Your precepts, for by them You have revived me.” Revived means given new life. He's saying God did it through those precepts, and that's why he won't forget them.

The text says it's true. The psalmist says, “I will never forget Your precepts, for by them You have revived me.” Revived is new life, and he says it came by God's precepts. So he has every reason to hold on to them.
Save him. He says, “I am Yours; save me, for I have sought Your precepts.” He starts with who he belongs to, and then he asks. That order matters.

Bless is a lovely word, but it's not in this verse. The psalmist says, “I am Yours; save me, for I have sought Your precepts.” What he asks for is saving. He's telling the LORD he belongs to Him, so he asks for rescue.

Forgive doesn't appear in this verse. He says, “I am Yours; save me, for I have sought Your precepts.” What he asks is to be saved. He gives his reason in the same breath: he has sought God's precepts.

It's the other way around, friend. The psalmist says, “I have seen a limit to all perfection, but Your commandment is without limit.” Everything else has a limit, and God's commandment doesn't. That little word “but” is doing the work.
False, you've got it. He says, “I have seen a limit to all perfection, but Your commandment is without limit.” He's seen limits everywhere else. God's commandment has none.
